is moved continuously over the entire length *Aa*; and the trapezium described by that motion, or the rectangle *Aa* x $\frac{1}{2}$ *a B* equal to it, will be equal to the sum of all the *MN* x *CM*, and therefore to the sum of all the *Dd* x *DK*, that is, to the area *BKVT a*. Which was to be demonstrated.

*Corollary.* From this, given the law of resistance and the difference *Aa* between the arcs *Ca* and *CB*, the proportion of the resistance to gravity can be gathered very nearly.

For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*; and from this, the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to $\frac{1}{2} Aa$. Therefore, since *DK* is the exponent of the resistance, and the length of the pendulum is the exponent of gravity, the resistance will be to gravity as $\frac{1}{2} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum; exactly as was demonstrated in proposition 28.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be an ellipsis very nearly. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, were to describe the length *BA* in a complete oscillation, the velocity in any place *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* of a circle described with diameter *AB*. Accordingly, since *Ba* in a resisting medium, and *BA* in a non-resisting medium, are described in approximately equal times; and therefore the velocities at each point of *Ba* are very nearly to the velocities at the corresponding points of the length *BA* as *Ba* is to *BA*; the velocity at point *D* in a resisting medium will be as the ordinate of a circle or ellipsis described upon the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be an ellipsis very nearly. Since the resistance is assumed proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the midpoint *O*; and the ellipsis *BRVSa*, with center *O* and semi-axes *OB*, *OV*, will very nearly equal the figure *BKVT a*, and the rectangle *Aa* x *BO* equal to it. Therefore, *Aa* x *BO* is to *OV* x *BO* as the area of this ellipsis is to *OV* x *BO*: that is, *Aa* to *OV* as the area of a semi-circle is to the square of the radius, or as 11 to 7 approximately: And for that reason $\frac{7}{11} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the duplicate ratio <note>The "duplicate ratio" of the velocity refers to the square of the velocity.</note> of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be almost a parabola having its vertex at *V* and axis *OV*, and therefore it will be equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV* very nearly. Therefore the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV*, and thus *OV* is equal to $\frac{3}{4} Aa$: and for that reason the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as $\frac{3}{4} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum.

<summary>Newton derives mathematical proportions for calculating the resistance of a medium against a pendulum. He shows how to determine the ratio of resistance to gravity for three cases: constant resistance, resistance proportional to velocity, and resistance proportional to the square of velocity.</summary>
